questions.problem: The function $y(t)$ gives the position of a particle at time $t>0.$ Which of the following equations represents a situation in which the particle is undergoing forced harmonic motion without damping?
questions.worked_solution:
The general equation of forced harmonic motion without damping is

$$
{y}^{″}+{\omega }^{2}y=f(t).
$$

We can see that the only equation that represents forced harmonic motion without damping is

$$
{y}^{″}+25y=4{t}^{2}.

questions.knowledge_point: Constructing a Differential Equation Governing a Forced Harmonic Motion
questions.problem:
A particle of mass $2\,\text{kg}$ is attached to a massless spring. The spring constant associated with the spring is $k=12\,{\text{kg/s}}^{2}.$ 
An external force $F(t)=10{e}^{2t}\,\text{N}$ is applied to the particle.

The position of the particle is $y(t)$ (measured in meters), and $t>0$ is the time in seconds. If the particle moves with forced harmonic motion without damping, what is the governing equation?
questions.worked_solution:
The equation of motion for a particle of mass $m$ moving with forced harmonic motion without damping under the action of a spring with spring constant $k$ and  external force $F(t)$ is given by

$$
m{y}^{″}=-ky+F(t).
$$

Substituting our values for $m,$ $k$ and $F(t)$ gives

$$
2{y}^{″}=-12y+10{e}^{2t}.
$$

Simplifying and rearranging the above equation, we get

$$
{y}^{″}+6y=5{e}^{2t}.
$$

The spring constant associated with the spring is $k=15\,{\text{kg/s}}^{2}.$  The particle is also subject to the resistive force that's proportional to the particle's velocity with a damping coefficient $c=12\,\text{kg/s},$ and an external force given by $F(t)=6{e}^{4t}\,\text{N}.$

m{y}^{″}=-c{y}^{′}-ky+F(t).

Substituting our values for $m,$ $k,$ $c$ and $F(t)$ gives

$$
3{y}^{″}=-12{y}^{′}-15y+6{e}^{4t}.
$$

Simplifying and rearranging the above equation, we get

$$
{y}^{″}+4{y}^{′}+5y=2{e}^{4t}.
$$

questions.knowledge_point: Identifying Solutions to Forced Harmonic Motion Equations
questions.problem:
A particle is moving with forced harmonic motion without damping. The position of the particle $y(t)$ at time $t$ is governed by the equation

$$
{y}^{″}+9y=10{e}^{-t}.
$$

Which of the following could be used to represent the general solution for $y(t)?$

- $y=R\operatorname{cos}⁡(3t+ϕ)+{e}^{-t}$
- $y=R\operatorname{sin}⁡(t+ϕ)+{e}^{-2t}$
- $y=A\operatorname{cos}⁡3t+B\operatorname{sin}⁡3t+{e}^{-t}$

Note that $A,$ $B,$ $R$ and $ϕ$ are constants.
questions.worked_solution:
The general solution to this equation is the sum of the complementary function and a particular solution.

First, we find the complementary solution ${y}_{c}(t),$ which is the solution to the simple harmonic motion equation ${y}^{″}+{\omega }^{2}y=0.$
It can be written in three different forms:

- ${y}_{c}=R\operatorname{cos}⁡(\omega t+ϕ)$

- ${y}_{c}=R\operatorname{sin}⁡(\omega t+ϕ)$

- ${y}_{c}=A\operatorname{cos}⁡\omega t+B\operatorname{sin}⁡\omega t$

In our case

$$
{\omega }^{2}=9\,⟹\,\omega =3.
$$

Thus, we have:

- ${y}_{c}=R\operatorname{cos}⁡(3t+ϕ)$

- ${y}_{c}=R\operatorname{sin}⁡(3t+ϕ)$

- ${y}_{c}=A\operatorname{cos}⁡3t+B\operatorname{sin}⁡3t$

Next, we find the particular solution ${y}_{p}(t).$ The particular solution is of the form

$$
{y}_{p}(t)=\alpha {e}^{-t}.
$$

By substituting the particular solution into the differential equation and equating coefficients, we find that $\alpha =1.$ So, the particular solution is

$$
{y}_{p}(t)={e}^{-t}.
$$

Finally, then, the general solution is given by the sum of the complementary and particular solutions. So, it can be written in any of the following forms:

- ${y}_{c}=R\operatorname{cos}⁡(3t+ϕ)+{e}^{-t}$

- ${y}_{c}=R\operatorname{sin}⁡(3t+ϕ)+{e}^{-t}$

- ${y}_{c}=A\operatorname{cos}⁡3t+B\operatorname{sin}⁡3t+{e}^{-t}$

Only I and III match the forms above. Therefore, the correct answer is "I and III only".

questions.problem:
A particle is moving with forced harmonic motion with damping. The position of the particle $y(t)$ at time $t$ is governed by the equation

$$
{y}^{″}+8{y}^{′}+41y=10{e}^{t}.
$$

Which of the following could be used to represent the general solution for $y(t)?$

- $y={e}^{-4t}(A\operatorname{cos}⁡5t+B\operatorname{sin}⁡5t)+\frac{{e}^{t}}{5}$
- $y=R\operatorname{sin}⁡(9t+ϕ)+\frac{{e}^{t}}{5}$
- $y=R{e}^{-4t}\operatorname{cos}⁡(5t+ϕ)+10{e}^{t}$

Note that $A,$ $B,$ $R$ and $ϕ$ are constants.
questions.worked_solution:
The general solution is the sum of the complementary solution and the particular solution:

$$
y(t)={y}_{c}(t)+{y}_{p}(t)
$$

First, we find the complementary solution ${y}_{c}(t),$ which is the solution to the homogeneous equation ${y}^{″}+8{y}^{′}+41y=0.$ Writing down and solving the characteristic equation gives

$$
\begin{aligned}{\lambda }^{2}+8\lambda +41 & =0 \\ ({\lambda }^{2}+8\lambda +16)-16+41 & =0 \\ (\lambda +4)^{2}+25 & =0 \\ (\lambda +4)^{2} & =-25 \\ \lambda +4 & =\pm 5\text{i} \\ \lambda  & =-4\pm 5\text{i}.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore the complementary function ${y}_{c}(t)$ can be expressed in any of the following forms:

$$
\begin{aligned}{y}_{c}(t) & ={e}^{-4t}(A\operatorname{cos}⁡5t+B\operatorname{sin}⁡5t), \\ {y}_{c}(t) & =R{e}^{-4t}\operatorname{sin}⁡(5t+ϕ), \\ {y}_{c}(t) & =R{e}^{-4t}\operatorname{cos}⁡(5t+ϕ).\end{aligned}
$$

Next, we find the particular solution ${y}_{p}(t).$ The particular solution is of the form

$$
{y}_{p}(t)=\alpha {e}^{t}.
$$

By substituting the particular solution into the differential equation and equating coefficients, we find that $\alpha =\frac{1}{5}.$ So, the particular solution is

$$
{y}_{p}(t)=\frac{{e}^{t}}{5}.
$$

Finally, then, the general solution is given by the sum of the complementary and particular solutions. So, it can be written in any of the following forms:

$$
\begin{aligned}y(t) & ={e}^{-4t}(A\operatorname{cos}⁡5t+B\operatorname{sin}⁡5t)+\frac{{e}^{t}}{5}, \\ y(t) & =R{e}^{-4t}\operatorname{sin}⁡(5t+ϕ)+\frac{{e}^{t}}{5}, \\ y(t) & =R{e}^{-4t}\operatorname{cos}⁡(5t+ϕ)+\frac{{e}^{t}}{5}.\end{aligned}
$$

Only I matches the forms above. Therefore, the correct answer is "I only".

$$

$$

Which of the following could be used to represent the general solution for $y(t)?$

- $y=R\operatorname{cos}⁡(t+ϕ)-t\operatorname{cos}⁡t$
- $y=R\operatorname{sin}⁡(t+ϕ)+2t\operatorname{sin}⁡t$
- $y=A\operatorname{cos}⁡t+B\operatorname{sin}⁡t-2t\operatorname{cos}⁡t+t\operatorname{sin}⁡t$

Note that $A,$ $B,$ $R$ and $ϕ$ are constants.
questions.worked_solution:
The general solution to this equation is the sum of the complementary function and a particular solution.

First, we find the complementary solution ${y}_{c}(t),$ which is the solution to the simple harmonic motion equation ${y}^{″}+{\omega }^{2}y=0.$

- ${y}_{c}=R\operatorname{cos}⁡(\omega t+ϕ)$

- ${y}_{c}=R\operatorname{sin}⁡(\omega t+ϕ)$

- ${y}_{c}=A\operatorname{cos}⁡\omega t+B\operatorname{sin}⁡\omega t$

In our case

$$
{\omega }^{2}=1\,⟹\,\omega =1.
$$

Thus, we have:

- ${y}_{c}=R\operatorname{cos}⁡(t+ϕ)$

- ${y}_{c}=R\operatorname{sin}⁡(t+ϕ)$

- ${y}_{c}=A\operatorname{cos}⁡t+B\operatorname{sin}⁡t$

Next, we find the particular solution ${y}_{p}(t).$ The particular solution is of the form

$$
{y}_{p}(t)=t(\alpha \operatorname{cos}⁡t+\beta \operatorname{sin}⁡t).
$$

By substituting the particular solution into the differential equation and equating coefficients, we find that $\alpha =-1$ and $\beta =0.$ So, the particular solution is

$$
{y}_{p}(t)=-t\operatorname{cos}⁡t.
$$

Finally, then, the general solution is given by the sum of the complementary and particular solutions. So, it can be written in any of the following forms:

- ${y}_{c}=R\operatorname{cos}⁡(t+ϕ)-t\operatorname{cos}⁡t$

- ${y}_{c}=R\operatorname{sin}⁡(t+ϕ)-t\operatorname{cos}⁡t$

- ${y}_{c}=A\operatorname{cos}⁡t+B\operatorname{sin}⁡t-t\operatorname{cos}⁡t$

Only I matches the forms above. Therefore, the correct answer is "I only".

Which of the following could be used to represent the general solution for $y(t)?$

- $y={e}^{-2t}(A\operatorname{cos}⁡4t+B\operatorname{sin}⁡4t)+10\operatorname{cos}⁡2t$
- $y=R{e}^{-4t}\operatorname{cos}⁡(t+ϕ)+2\operatorname{cos}⁡2t+\operatorname{sin}⁡2t$
- $y=R{e}^{-2t}\operatorname{sin}⁡(4t+ϕ)+2\operatorname{cos}⁡2t+\operatorname{sin}⁡2t$

$$
y(t)={y}_{c}(t)+{y}_{p}(t)

$$
\begin{aligned}{\lambda }^{2}+4\lambda +20 & =0 \\ ({\lambda }^{2}+4\lambda +4)-4+20 & =0 \\ (\lambda +2)^{2}+16 & =0 \\ (\lambda +2)^{2} & =-16 \\ \lambda +2 & =\pm 4\text{i} \\ \lambda  & =-2\pm 4\text{i}.\end{aligned}

$$
\begin{aligned}{y}_{c}(t) & ={e}^{-2t}(A\operatorname{cos}⁡4t+B\operatorname{sin}⁡4t), \\ {y}_{c}(t) & =R{e}^{-2t}\operatorname{cos}⁡(4t+ϕ), \\ {y}_{c}(t) & =R{e}^{-2t}\operatorname{sin}⁡(4t+ϕ).\end{aligned}
$$

$$
{y}_{p}(t)=\alpha \operatorname{cos}⁡2t+\beta \operatorname{sin}⁡2t.
$$

By substituting the particular solution into the differential equation and equating coefficients, we find that $\alpha =2$ and $\beta =1.$ So, the particular solution is

$$
{y}_{p}(t)=2\operatorname{cos}⁡2t+\operatorname{sin}⁡2t.
$$

$$
\begin{aligned}y(t) & ={e}^{-2t}(A\operatorname{cos}⁡4t+B\operatorname{sin}⁡4t)+2\operatorname{cos}⁡2t+\operatorname{sin}⁡2t, \\ y(t) & =R{e}^{-2t}\operatorname{cos}⁡(4t+ϕ)+2\operatorname{cos}⁡2t+\operatorname{sin}⁡2t, \\ y(t) & =R{e}^{-2t}\operatorname{sin}⁡(4t+ϕ)+2\operatorname{cos}⁡2t+\operatorname{sin}⁡2t.\end{aligned}

questions.knowledge_point: Calculating the Position of a Particle Oscillating With Forced Harmonic Motion at a Moment
questions.problem:
The position $y(t),$ measured in meters, of a particle oscillating with forced harmonic motion with light damping is governed by the equation

$$
{y}^{″}+4{y}^{′}+8y=8-16t,
$$

where $t>0$ is the time, in seconds. Given that the particle is initially at $y=2\,\text{m}$ with zero velocity, find the position of the particle after $\frac{\pi }{4}$ seconds.
questions.worked_solution:
The general solution to the equation of forced harmonic motion with light damping is the sum of the complementary function and a particular solution.

The complementary solution ${y}_{c}$ is the solution to the homogeneous equation

$$
{y}^{″}+4{y}^{′}+8y=0.
$$

Writing down and solving the auxiliary equation gives

$$
\begin{aligned}{\lambda }^{2}+4\lambda +8 & =0 \\ (\lambda +2)^{2}+4 & =0 \\ (\lambda +2)^{2} & =-4 \\ \lambda +2 & =\pm 2\text{i} \\ \lambda  & =-2\pm 2\text{i}.\end{aligned}
$$

Thus, we have

$$
{y}_{c}={e}^{-2t}(P\operatorname{cos}⁡2t+Q\operatorname{sin}⁡2t).
$$

We now need to find the particular integral ${y}_{p}(t).$

The external force is a linear polynomial. Therefore, we assume that the particular integral is also a linear polynomial, i.e.

$$
{y}_{p}=\alpha +\beta t,
$$

where $\alpha ,$ $\beta $ are constants to be determined. 

Substituting ${y}_{p}$ into the differential equation and equating coefficients gives $\alpha =2,$ $\beta =-2.$

Therefore, the particular solution ${y}_{p}(t)$ is

$$
{y}_{p}(t)=2-2t,
$$

and the general solution is

$$
y={e}^{-2t}(P\operatorname{cos}⁡2t+Q\operatorname{sin}⁡2t)+2-2t.
$$

Since the particle is initially at $y=2\,\text{m}$ with zero velocity, the initial conditions are $y(0)=2$ and ${y}^{′}(0)=0.$

Solving with these conditions for $P$ and $Q$ gives

$$
P=0,\,Q=1.
$$

So our solution is

$$
y(t)={e}^{-2t}\operatorname{sin}⁡2t+2-2t.
$$

To find the position of the particle after $\frac{\pi }{4}$ seconds, we substitute into the equation $t=\frac{\pi }{4}.$ We get

$$
\begin{aligned}y(\frac{\pi }{4}) & ={e}^{-2(\pi /4)}\operatorname{sin}⁡(2\cdot \frac{\pi }{4})+2-2(\frac{\pi }{4}) \\  & =({e}^{-\pi /2}+2-\frac{\pi }{2})\,\text{m}.\end{aligned}
$$

questions.problem:
The position $y(t),$ measured in meters, of a particle oscillating with forced harmonic motion without damping is governed by the equation

$$
{y}^{″}+4y=8{t}^{2},
$$

where $t>0$ is the time, in seconds. Given that the particle is initially at the origin with zero velocity, find the position of the particle after $1$ second.
questions.worked_solution:
The general solution to the equation of forced harmonic motion without damping is the sum of the complementary function and a particular solution.

The complementary solution ${y}_{c}$ represents simple harmonic motion and can be written as

$$
{y}_{c}=A\operatorname{cos}⁡\omega t+B\operatorname{sin}⁡\omega t,
$$

where $A$ and $B$ are arbitrary constants of integration.

In our case,

$$
{\omega }^{2}=4\,⟹\,\omega =2.
$$

Thus, we have

$$
{y}_{c}=A\operatorname{cos}⁡2t+B\operatorname{sin}⁡2t.
$$

We now need to find the particular integral ${y}_{p}(t).$

The external force is a polynomial of degree $2.$ Therefore, we assume that the particular integral is also a polynomial of degree $2,$ i.e.,

$$
{y}_{p}=\alpha {t}^{2}+\beta t+\gamma 
$$

where $\alpha ,$ $\beta $ and $\gamma $ are constants that are to be determined. 

Substituting ${y}_{p}$ into the differential equation and equating coefficients gives $\alpha =2,\beta =0,\gamma =-1.$

Therefore, the particular solution ${y}_{p}(t)$ is

$$
{y}_{p}(t)=2{t}^{2}-1,
$$

and the general solution is

$$
y=A\operatorname{cos}⁡2t+B\operatorname{sin}⁡2t+2{t}^{2}-1.
$$

Since the particle is initially at the origin with zero velocity, the initial conditions are $y(0)=0$ and ${y}^{′}(0)=0.$

Solving with these conditions for $A$ and $B$ gives

$$
A=1,\,B=0.
$$

So our solution is

$$
y(t)=\operatorname{cos}⁡2t+2{t}^{2}-1.
$$

To find the position of the particle after one second, we substitute into the equation $t=1.$ We get

$$
\begin{aligned}y(1) & =\operatorname{cos}⁡2(1)+2(1)^{2}-1 \\  & =(\operatorname{cos}⁡2+1)\,\text{m}.\end{aligned}
$$

The position $y(t),$ measured in inches, of a particle oscillating with forced harmonic motion with light damping is governed by the equation

$$
{y}^{″}+2{y}^{′}+5y=34\operatorname{cos}⁡2t,
$$

where $t>0$ is the time, in seconds. Given that the particle is initially at the origin with zero velocity, find the position of the particle after $\pi $ seconds.
questions.worked_solution:
The general solution to the equation of forced harmonic motion with light damping is the sum of the complementary function and a particular solution.

The complementary solution ${y}_{c}$ is the solution to the homogeneous equation

$$
{y}^{″}+2{y}^{′}+5y=0.
$$

Writing down and solving the auxiliary equation gives

$$
\begin{aligned}{\lambda }^{2}+2\lambda +5 & =0 \\ (\lambda +1)^{2}+4 & =0 \\ (\lambda +1)^{2} & =-4 \\ \lambda +1 & =\pm 2\text{i} \\ \lambda  & =-1\pm 2\text{i}.\end{aligned}
$$

Thus, we have

$$
{y}_{c}={e}^{-t}(P\operatorname{cos}⁡2t+Q\operatorname{sin}⁡2t).
$$

where $P$ and $Q$ are arbitrary constants of integration.

We now need to find the particular integral ${y}_{p}(t).$

The external force is $34\operatorname{cos}⁡2t.$ Therefore, we assume that the particular integral is

$$
{y}_{p}=\alpha \operatorname{cos}⁡2t+\beta \operatorname{sin}⁡2t,
$$

where $\alpha ,$ $\beta $ are constants to be determined. 

Substituting ${y}_{p}$ into the differential equation and equating coefficients gives $\alpha =2,$ $\beta =8.$

Therefore, the particular solution ${y}_{p}(t)$ is

$$
{y}_{p}(t)=2\operatorname{cos}⁡2t+8\operatorname{sin}⁡2t,
$$

and the general solution is

$$
y={e}^{-t}(P\operatorname{cos}⁡2t+Q\operatorname{sin}⁡2t)+2\operatorname{cos}⁡2t+8\operatorname{sin}⁡2t.
$$

Since the particle is initially at the origin with zero velocity, the initial conditions are $y(0)=0$ and ${y}^{′}(0)=0.$

Solving with these conditions for $P$ and $Q$ gives

$$
P=-2,\,Q=-9.
$$

So our solution is

$$
y(t)=2\operatorname{cos}⁡2t+8\operatorname{sin}⁡2t-{e}^{-t}(2\operatorname{cos}⁡2t+9\operatorname{sin}⁡2t).
$$

To find the position of the particle after $\pi $ seconds, we substitute into the equation $t=\pi .$ We get

$$
\begin{aligned}y(\pi ) & =2\operatorname{cos}⁡(2\pi )+8\operatorname{sin}⁡(2\pi )-{e}^{-\pi }(2\operatorname{cos}⁡(2\pi )+9\operatorname{sin}⁡(2\pi )) \\  & =2(1-{e}^{-\pi })\,\text{in}.\end{aligned}
$$

questions.problem:
The position $y(t),$ measured in centimeters, of a particle oscillating with forced harmonic motion without damping is governed by the equation

$$
{y}^{″}+49y=-24\operatorname{cos}⁡t,
$$

where $t>0$ is the time, in seconds. Given that the particle is initially at the origin with zero velocity, find the position of the particle after $\frac{\pi }{2}$ seconds.
questions.worked_solution:
The general solution to the equation of forced harmonic motion without damping is the sum of the complementary function and a particular solution.

The complementary solution ${y}_{c}$ represents simple harmonic motion and can be written as

$$
{y}_{c}=A\operatorname{cos}⁡\omega t+B\operatorname{sin}⁡\omega t,
$$

where $A$ and $B$ are arbitrary constants of integration.

In our case,

$$
{\omega }^{2}=49\,⟹\,\omega =7.
$$

Thus, we have

$$
{y}_{c}=A\operatorname{cos}⁡7t+B\operatorname{sin}⁡7t.
$$

We now need to find the particular integral ${y}_{p}(t).$

The external force is $-24\operatorname{cos}⁡t.$ Therefore, we assume that the particular integral is

$$
{y}_{p}=\alpha \operatorname{cos}⁡t+\beta \operatorname{sin}⁡t,
$$

where $\alpha ,\beta $ are constants to be determined.

Substituting ${y}_{p}$ into the differential equation and equating coefficients gives $\alpha =-\frac{1}{2},\beta =0.$

Therefore, the particular solution ${y}_{p}(t)$ is

$$
{y}_{p}(t)=-\frac{1}{2}\operatorname{cos}⁡t,
$$

and the general solution is

$$
y=A\operatorname{cos}⁡7t+B\operatorname{sin}⁡7t-\frac{1}{2}\operatorname{cos}⁡t.
$$

Since the particle is initially at the origin with zero velocity, the initial conditions are $y(0)=0$ and ${y}^{′}(0)=0.$

Solving with these conditions for $A$ and $B$ gives

$$
A=\frac{1}{2},\,B=0.
$$

So our solution is

$$
y(t)=\frac{1}{2}\operatorname{cos}⁡7t-\frac{1}{2}\operatorname{cos}⁡t.
$$

To find the position of the particle after $\frac{\pi }{2}$ seconds, we substitute into the equation $t=\frac{\pi }{2}.$ We get

$$
\begin{aligned}y(\frac{\pi }{2}) & =\frac{1}{2}\operatorname{cos}⁡(\frac{7\pi }{2})-\frac{1}{2}\operatorname{cos}⁡(\frac{\pi }{2})=0\,\text{cm}.\end{aligned}
$$

questions.problem:
The position $y(t),$ measured in meters, of a particle oscillating with forced harmonic motion without damping is governed by the equation

$$
{y}^{″}+9y=12\operatorname{cos}⁡3t,
$$

where $t>0$ is the time, in seconds. Given that the particle is initially at the origin with velocity $3\,\frac{\text{m}}{\text{s}}$, find the position of the particle after $\frac{\pi }{6}$ seconds.
questions.worked_solution:
The general solution to the equation of forced harmonic motion without damping is the sum of the complementary function and a particular solution.

The complementary solution ${y}_{c}$ represents simple harmonic motion and can be written as

$$
{y}_{c}=A\operatorname{cos}⁡\omega t+B\operatorname{sin}⁡\omega t,
$$

where $A$ and $B$ are arbitrary constants of integration.

In our case,

$$
{\omega }^{2}=9\,⟹\,\omega =3.
$$

Thus, we have

$$
{y}_{c}=A\operatorname{cos}⁡3t+B\operatorname{sin}⁡3t.
$$

We now need to find the particular integral ${y}_{p}(t).$

The external force is $12\operatorname{cos}⁡3t.$ The particular solution of the inhomogeneous equation cannot be of the form $\alpha \operatorname{cos}⁡3t+\beta \operatorname{sin}⁡3t$ because this is already included in the complimentary function. Therefore, we assume that the particular integral is  

$$
{y}_{p}=t(\alpha \operatorname{cos}⁡3t+\beta \operatorname{sin}⁡3t),
$$

where $\alpha $ and $\beta $ are constants that are to be determined.  

Substituting ${y}_{p}$ into the differential equation and equating coefficients gives $\alpha =0,\beta =2.$

Therefore, the particular solution ${y}_{p}(t)$ is

$$
{y}_{p}(t)=2t\operatorname{sin}⁡3t,
$$

and the general solution is

$$
y=A\operatorname{cos}⁡3t+B\operatorname{sin}⁡3t+2t\operatorname{sin}⁡3t=A\operatorname{cos}⁡3t+(B+2t)\operatorname{sin}⁡3t.
$$

Since the particle is initially at the origin with velocity $3\,\frac{\text{m}}{\text{s}}$, the initial conditions are $y(0)=0$ and ${y}^{′}(0)=3.$

Solving with these conditions for $A$ and $B$ gives

$$
A=0,\,B=1.
$$

So our solution is

$$
y(t)=(1+2t)\operatorname{sin}⁡3t.
$$

To find the position of the particle after $\frac{\pi }{6}$ seconds, we substitute into the equation $t=\frac{\pi }{6}.$ We get

$$
\begin{aligned}y(\frac{\pi }{6}) & =(1+2\cdot \frac{\pi }{6})\operatorname{sin}⁡\frac{\pi }{2} \\  & =(1+\frac{\pi }{3})\,\text{m}.\end{aligned}
$$

canonical_examples.knowledge_point: Identifying Equations that Represent Forced Harmonic Motion
canonical_examples.problem:
The function $y(t)$ gives the position of a particle at time $t > 0.$ Determine whether each equation is forced or free, and whether it is damped.

- $y''+y'+3y = t$

- $y''+ 4y = e^t$

- $y''+y'+3y = 0$
canonical_examples.worked_solution:
The differential equation

$$
y'' + b y' + \omega^2 y = f(t)
$$

is forced if $f(t)$ is not identical to zero, and damped if $b>0.$

With that in mind, let's classify each equation.

- Equation I represents forced harmonic motion with damping. The forcing function $f(t)=t$ is not always zero, and there is a damping term with $b=1>0.$

- Equation II represents forced harmonic motion without damping. The forcing function $f(t)=e^t$ is not always zero, but there is no damping term since $b=0.$

- Equation III represents free (non-forced) harmonic motion with damping. The forcing function $f(t)=0$ is always zero, and there is a damping term with $b=1>0.$

canonical_examples.knowledge_point: Constructing a Differential Equation Governing a Forced Harmonic Motion
canonical_examples.problem:
A particle of mass $3\,\textrm{kg}$ is attached to a massless spring. The spring constant associated with the spring is $k = 6\, \textrm{kg/s}^2.$  The particle is also subject to the resistive force that's proportional to the particle's velocity with a damping coefficient $c = 9\, \textrm{kg/s},$ and an external force given by $F(t)=3t^2\,\textrm{N}.$   

The position of the particle is $y(t)$ (measured in meters), and $t>0$ is the time in seconds.  If the particle moves with forced harmonic motion, what is the governing equation?
canonical_examples.worked_solution:
The general equation of forced harmonic motion with damping is

$$
m y'' =-cy' -k y + F(t) .
$$

Substituting our values for $m,$ $k,$ $c$ and $F(t)$ gives

$$
3 y'' =-9y' -6 y+3t^2.
$$

Simplifying and rearranging the above equation, we get

$$
y'' + 3y'+2y = t^2.
$$

canonical_examples.knowledge_point: Identifying Solutions to Forced Harmonic Motion Equations
canonical_examples.problem:
A particle is moving with forced harmonic motion with damping. The position of the particle $y(t)$ at time $t$ is governed by the equation

$$
y''+2y' + 5 y = 50t.
$$

Which of the following could be used to represent the general solution for $y(t)?$

- $y =Ae^{-t}+Be^{-2t}+25t+5$

- $y = R e ^ {- t} \cos \left( 2t + \phi \right) +10t - 4$

- $y =e^{-t}\left( A\cos{2t} + B\sin{2t}\right)+10 t-4$

Note that $A$ and $B$ are constants.
canonical_examples.worked_solution:
The general solution is the sum of the complementary solution and the particular solution:

$$
y(t) = y_c(t)+y_p(t)
$$

First, we find the complementary solution $y_c(t),$ which is the solution to the homogeneous equation $y''+2y' + 5 y = 0.$ Writing down and solving the characteristic equation gives

$$
\begin{aligned}{\lambda }^{2}+2\lambda +5 & =0 \\ ({\lambda }^{2}+2\lambda +1)-1+5 & =0 \\ (\lambda +1)^{2}+4 & =0 \\ (\lambda +1)^{2} & =-4 \\ \lambda +1 & =\pm 2\text{i} \\ \lambda  & =-1\pm 2\text{i}.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore the complementary function $y_c(t)$ is can be expressed in any of the following forms:

$$
\begin{aligned}{y}_{c}(t) & ={e}^{-t}(A\operatorname{cos}⁡2t+B\operatorname{sin}⁡2t), \\ {y}_{c}(t) & =R{e}^{-t}\operatorname{cos}⁡(2t+ϕ), \\ {y}_{c}(t) & =R{e}^{-t}\operatorname{sin}⁡(2t+ϕ).\end{aligned}
$$

Next, we find the particular solution $y_p(t).$ Note that the external force $f(t)=50t$ is a linear function. Therefore, we assume that the particular solution is also a linear function,

$$
y_p(t)=\alpha t+\beta.
$$

By substituting the particular solution into the differential equation and equating coefficients, we find that $\alpha = 10$ and $\beta = -4.$ So, the particular solution is

$$
y_p(t)= 10 t - 4.
$$

Finally, then, the general solution is given by the sum of the complementary and particular solutions. So, it can be written in any of the following forms:

$$
\begin{aligned}y(t) & ={e}^{-t}(A\operatorname{cos}⁡2t+B\operatorname{sin}⁡2t)+10t-4, \\ y(t) & =R{e}^{-t}\operatorname{cos}⁡(2t+ϕ)+10t-4, \\ y(t) & =R{e}^{-t}\operatorname{sin}⁡(2t+ϕ)+10t-4.\end{aligned}
$$

Only II and III match the forms above. Therefore, the correct answer is "II and III only".

canonical_examples.knowledge_point: Calculating the Position of a Particle Oscillating With Forced Harmonic Motion at a Moment
canonical_examples.problem:
The position $y(t),$ measured in meters, of a particle oscillating with forced harmonic motion without damping is governed by the equation

$$
y'' + y =2e^{-t},
$$

where $t > 0$ is the time, in seconds. Given that the particle is initially at the origin with zero velocity, find the position of the particle after $\pi$ seconds.
canonical_examples.worked_solution:
This is an initial value problem. Since the particle is initially at the origin with zero velocity, the initial conditions are $y(0)=0$ and $y'(0)=0.$ So, we want to solve the initial value problem

$$
y'' + y =2e^{-t}, \quad y(0)=0, \quad y'(0)=0.
$$

First, we find the general solution of the differential equation. The complementary solution $y_c(t)$ represents simple harmonic motion and can be written as

$$
y_c=A\cos{\omega t} + B\sin{\omega t}.
$$

In our case,

$$
\omega^2 = 1\qquad\Longrightarrow\qquad \omega = 1,
$$

so we have

$$
y_c=A\cos{t} + B\sin{t}.
$$

Next, we find the particular solution $y_p(t).$ Note that the external force $f(t) = 2e^{-t}$ is an exponential function, and the constant factor in the exponent $(-1)$ is not a root of the auxiliary equation. Therefore, we assume a particular exponential solution of the form 

$$
y_p = \alpha  e^{-t},
$$

where $\alpha$ is a constant to be determined. 

Substituting $y_p$ into the differential equation and equating coefficients gives $\alpha=1.$ Therefore, the particular solution $y_p(t)$ is

$$
y_p(t) =e^{-t},
$$

and the general solution is

$$
y=A\cos{t} + B\sin{t} + e^{-t}.
$$

Finally, we find the constants $A$ and $B$ using the initial conditions. Substituting $y(0)=0$ gives $A=-1,$ and differentiating $y$ and substituting $y'(0)=0$ gives $B=1.$

So, our solution is

$$
y(t)=-\cos t + \sin{t} +e^{-t}.
$$

To find the position of the particle after $\pi$ seconds, we substitute into the equation $t=\pi$ and get

$$
\begin{aligned}y(\pi ) & =-\operatorname{cos}⁡\pi +\operatorname{sin}⁡\pi +{e}^{-\pi } \\  & =(1+{e}^{-\pi })\,\text{m}.\end{aligned}
$$
